content.heading: 6.2 Orthogonal Sets
content.paragraph: A set of vectors $\left\{ \mathbf{u}_{1}\text{,~}\ldots\text{,~}\mathbf{u}_{p} \right\}$ in $\text{ℝ}^{n}$ is said to be an orthogonal set if each pair of distinct vectors from the set is orthogonal, that is, if $\mathbf{u}_{i} \cdot \mathbf{u}_{j} = 0$ whenever $i \neq j$.

note.title: Definition
note.heading: Definition
note.paragraph: An orthogonal basis for a subspace $W$ of $\text{ℝ}^{n}$ is a basis for $W$ that is also an orthogonal set.

content.paragraph: The next theorem suggests why an orthogonal basis is much nicer than other bases. The weights in a linear combination can be computed easily.

content.heading: A Geometric Interpretation of Theorem 5
content.paragraph: The formula for the orthogonal projection $\widehat{\textbf{y}}$ in (2) has the same appearance as each of the terms in Theorem 5. Thus Theorem 5 decomposes a vector $\textbf{y}$ into a sum of orthogonal projections onto one-dimensional subspaces.

It is easy to visualize the case in which $W = \text{ℝ}^{2} = \text{Span~}\left\{ \mathbf{u}_{1}\text{,~}\mathbf{u}_{2} \right\}$, with $\mathbf{u}_{1}$ and $\mathbf{u}_{2}$ orthogonal. Any $\textbf{y}$ in $\text{ℝ}^{2}$ can be written in the form

The first term in (3) is the projection of $\textbf{y}$ onto the subspace spanned by $\mathbf{u}_{1}$ (the line through $\mathbf{u}_{1}$ and the origin), and the second term is the projection of $\textbf{y}$ onto the subspace spanned by $\mathbf{u}_{2}$. Thus (3) expresses $\textbf{y}$ as the sum of its projections onto the (orthogonal) axes determined by $\mathbf{u}_{1}$ and $\mathbf{u}_{2}$. See Figure 4.

content.paragraph: Theorem 5 decomposes each $\textbf{y}$ in $\text{Span~}\left\{ \mathbf{u}_{1}\text{,~}\ldots\text{,~}\mathbf{u}_{p} \right\}$ into the sum of $p$ projections onto one-dimensional subspaces that are mutually orthogonal.
content.heading: Decomposing a Force into Component Forces
content.paragraph: The decomposition in Figure 4 can occur in physics when some sort of force is applied to an object. Choosing an appropriate coordinate system allows the force to be represented by a vector $\textbf{y}$ in $\text{ℝ}^{2}$ or $\text{ℝ}^{3}$. Often the problem involves some particular direction of interest, which is represented by another vector $\mathbf{u}$. For instance, if the object is moving in a straight line when the force is applied, the vector $\mathbf{u}$ might point in the direction of movement, as in Figure 5. A key step in the problem is to decompose the force into a component in the direction of $\mathbf{u}$ and a component orthogonal to $\mathbf{u}$. The calculations would be analogous to those previously made in Example 3.

content.heading: Orthonormal Sets
content.paragraph: A set $\left\{ \mathbf{u}_{1}\text{,~}\ldots\text{,~}\mathbf{u}_{p} \right\}$ is an orthonormal set if it is an orthogonal set of unit vectors. If $W$ is the subspace spanned by such a set, then $\left\{ \mathbf{u}_{1}\text{,~}\ldots\text{,~}\mathbf{u}_{p} \right\}$ is an orthonormal basis for $W$, since the set is automatically linearly independent, by Theorem 4.

The simplest example of an orthonormal set is the standard basis $\left\{ \textbf{e}_{1}\text{,~}\ldots\text{,~}\textbf{e}_{n} \right\}$ for $\text{ℝ}^{n}$. Any nonempty subset of $\left\{ \textbf{e}_{1}\text{,~}\ldots\text{,~}\textbf{e}_{n} \right\}$ is orthonormal, too. Here is a more complicated example.

content.paragraph: When the vectors in an orthogonal set of nonzero vectors are normalized to have unit length, the new vectors will still be orthogonal, and hence the new set will be an orthonormal set. See Exercise 40. It is easy to check that the vectors in Figure 6 (Example ﻿﻿5) are simply the unit vectors in the directions of the vectors in Figure 1 (Example ﻿1).
Matrices whose columns form an orthonormal set are important in applications and in computer algorithms for matrix computations. Their main properties are given in Theorems 6 and 7.

content.paragraph: Theorem 6 and 7 are particularly useful when applied to square matrices. An orthogonal matrix is a square invertible matrix $U$ such that $U^{- 1} = U^{T}$. By Theorem 6, such a matrix has orthonormal columns.1 It is easy to see that any square matrix with orthonormal columns is an orthogonal matrix. Surprisingly, such a matrix must have orthonormal rows, too. See Exercises 35 and 36. Orthogonal matrices will appear frequently in Chapter 7.
